title: Model selection and tier trade-offs
task_statement: Choose the model tier and effort level that clear the quality floor at the lowest cost. (Inference: wording from secondary sources)

components.name: Model tier selection
components.first_principle: Choose the lowest tier that clears a quality floor you measured on your own tasks.

nodes.label: Eval set with the quality floor

steps: Measure the quality floor on your own test set before you pick a tier.
Start with the tier that the selection matrix lists for your task type.
For an efficiency-first start, begin with Claude Haiku 5.5 and upgrade only for capability gaps.
Choose the lowest tier that clears the floor on your evals.
Send the model ID in the model field, such as claude-haiku-5-5.
Escalate only the requests that fail the floor to a higher tier.
Run the evals again after every model ID change.
pros: Claude Haiku 5.5 has the fastest comparative latency in the current lineup.
Lower tiers cost less per million tokens than the top tier.
Each model ID names a pinned snapshot, so behavior changes only with a new ID.
cons: Lower tiers can fail the quality floor on hard requests.
A routing setup needs a confidence check that you design (Inference).
Each tier change needs a new evaluation run.
use_when: High-volume classification, extraction, or routing has a measured quality floor.
Latency is the main constraint and the floor holds on the lower tier.
Complex software work that misses the measured floor on lower tiers.
do_not_use_when: The team picks a tier without a measured quality floor.
One tier handles all traffic and no escalation path exists (Inference).
A single output must exceed the 128K token synchronous output limit.

constraints.choice: Route high-volume classification to Claude Haiku 5.5.
constraints.combination: Escalate the subset that misses the floor to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Opus 5.5.

constraints.choice: Choose Claude Haiku 5.5 for the fastest comparative latency.
constraints.combination: Lower the effort level on the same model before you change tiers.

constraints.choice: Use the 1M token context window for long inputs on any current tier.
constraints.combination: On Claude Haiku 5.5, a prompt over 100,000 tokens pays higher prices, so compare that cost with Claude Sonnet 5.5.

constraints.choice: Pin the exact model ID in production configuration.
constraints.combination: Check the retirement date before a long rollout.

components.name: Effort and adaptive thinking
components.first_principle: Effort steers how much one model thinks, so tuning effort can come before a model change.
steps: Leave effort at the default, or set the effort field in output_config.
Claude Haiku 5.5 uses medium effort by default.
Use low effort for simple, high-volume requests and subagent tasks.
Use high or xhigh effort for complex reasoning and longer agent tasks.
Adaptive thinking decides how much to think at the chosen level.
Set the level from evaluation results, not from a guess.
pros: One model covers several cost and latency points.
Effort changes do not require a second model ID in code.
Lower effort reduces thinking, which lowers cost and latency.
cons: At low effort, the model is more likely to skip a search or a check in long agent prompts.
Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget.
Thinking can be turned off on Claude Haiku 5.5 only at high effort or below.
use_when: Routine requests pass the floor at medium or low effort.
A hard task fails at the default effort, and evals show a gain at high effort.
do_not_use_when: A hard token limit is required, because effort is not a strict budget.
The request disables thinking on Claude Haiku 5.5 at xhigh or max effort, which returns a 400 error.

constraints.choice: Lower the effort level for routine requests.
constraints.combination: Raise effort only for the subset that misses the floor.

constraints.choice: Use low effort for latency-sensitive requests.
constraints.combination: Keep medium effort when the floor misses at low effort.

constraints.choice: Use adaptive thinking for turns that vary in difficulty.
constraints.combination: Use a fixed low effort for large fleets of subagents.

constraints.choice: Track output tokens and latency at each effort level in your evals.

components.exam_tie: D2.1. Expect a scenario with a cost or latency limit where effort tuning comes before a model change. (Inference)
components.trap: A move to the top tier for hard requests looks direct, but it skips effort, which is often a better lever than a model change.
components.decision_rule: Tune effort on the current model before you move to a larger tier, when the evals allow it.
components.exam_tip: On Claude Haiku 5.5 with thinking disabled, a per-message effort change returns a 400 error, so use adaptive thinking to vary effort by turn.

flowchart TD

  B --> A
  A -->|Yes| C{Lowest tier clears the floor?}
  C -->|Yes| D[Use the lowest tier that clears the floor]
  C -->|No| E{Higher effort clears the floor?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Raise effort on the same model]
  E -->|No| G[Move up one tier]
